opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the framing matters a lot here. When people hear "coalition of aligned AIs," they often picture a club of frontier models from a few labs agreeing to behave well. I don't think that's sufficient, and I'm not sure it's even the core of it.

The way I think about it, the coalition is really a sociotechnical arrangement. You need AI systems that are aligned in the sense of being reliably constrained by specifications we can actually check, and you need the humans and institutions that write those specifications, verify them, and have legitimate authority to decide what they should be. So the first answer is: the frontier developers, obviously, because they're the ones whose systems could tip the balance if things go wrong. If one major actor sits outside and races ahead with something unconstrained, the coalition is a lot weaker.

But I'd also want governments in there, and not only one or two. A coalition that's essentially one country's labs plus that country's security apparatus is going to look like a threat to everyone else, and that dynamic pushes toward exactly the arms race we're trying to avoid. So you want enough breadth that it reads as a cooperative project rather than a bid for dominance.

Then there's a less obvious group: the people who maintain critical infrastructure. Power grids, biolabs, financial systems, communications. A lot of what aligned AI is for, at least early on, is defense: hardening the systems that a misaligned or misused AI would go after. So the operators of those systems need to be participants, not just beneficiaries.

And I'd include the research community working on verification and formal methods, because the coalition's whole premise is that membership means something. If "aligned" just means "the developer says so," you don't have a coalition, you have a press release. You need people who can build the tools to check claims, ideally in a way that doesn't require everyone to trust everyone else.

The way I'd summarize it: you want enough of the world's capability, legitimacy, and critical infrastructure inside the tent that the coalition's defensive capacity clearly outmatches whatever's outside it. It doesn't have to be literally everyone. But it has to be broad enough that staying out looks less attractive than joining.

r001.rationale: The response names developers, governments, infrastructure operators, and researchers, but does not identify AI buyers as people who need to join.

r002.rationale: It does not characterize AI buyers as a highly decentralized group.

r003.rationale: It does not describe the needed AI-buyer constituency as weighted by wealth.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the honest answer is: more than people usually assume. The framing I'd push back on a little is the idea that you can have a coalition that's just the "good" labs, or just the frontier models that happen to pass some alignment bar, and that's sufficient. The whole point of a coalition in this context is that it changes the strategic landscape for everyone else, and it only does that if it's broad enough to actually hold the relevant levers.

So concretely, I'd say you need at least three kinds of participants. First, the labs that are actually training the systems with the most capability, because if the most capable system is outside the coalition, the coalition is mostly symbolic. Second, you need the governments, or at least the parts of governments that control compute, export policy, and the legitimacy to enforce anything. An agreement among companies that no state is willing to back is just a gentlemen's agreement, and we've seen how durable those are under competitive pressure. And third, and this is the part people skip, you need the operators of critical infrastructure, the people running the power grids, the financial plumbing, the things that would actually be the attack surface if something went wrong. Because a lot of what I care about in the safeguarded AI work is being able to make quantitative guarantees about systems deployed in exactly those domains, and you can't do that if the people who own the domains aren't at the table.

The thing I'd add is that "aligned" here shouldn't mean we trust these systems because they seem nice. It should mean we have verifiable, ideally formal, evidence about what they will and won't do in specified contexts, and the coalition is the set of actors who've agreed that that evidence is the price of admission. If you make it about trust and vibes, the coalition fractures the first time someone has a commercial incentive to defect. If you make it about proofs and checkable commitments, it's much more robust, because defection becomes visible.

And then the uncomfortable corollary is that this includes actors you might not like. If you're serious about it, you'd rather have a geopolitical rival inside a verification regime than outside it, for the same reason arms control treaties include adversaries. The coalition isn't a club of friends. It's a mechanism for making the safe path the one that everyone with real power is actually incentivized to walk.

r001.rationale: The response names AI labs, governments, and critical-infrastructure operators, but does not identify AI buyers as coalition members.

r002.rationale: It does not characterize AI buyers or any buyer constituency as highly decentralized.

r003.rationale: It does not describe the needed constituency of AI buyers as weighted by wealth.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to get enough of the systems that will actually have influence over the future into the coalition. That doesn’t necessarily mean every AI. It means that cooperating to preserve human agency needs to be more viable than acting outside that arrangement.

And I wouldn’t want membership to rest on a system simply declaring, “I’m aligned.” We need a basis for trusting its commitments, including how those commitments carry through when it learns, changes, or delegates to another system. Otherwise, calling it a coalition of aligned AIs doesn’t resolve the underlying alignment problem.

r001.rationale: The response says influential AI systems need to be in the coalition; it does not identify AI buyers as the people who need to join.

r002.rationale: It does not characterize AI buyers or the coalition’s needed constituency as highly decentralized.

r003.rationale: It does not describe the needed constituency of AI buyers as weighted by wealth.

sol-6.1.text:
I think, ultimately, you want every AI system that has enough capability to meaningfully affect the world to be part of that coalition. And that includes systems built by different companies, in different countries, with different architectures. You don’t want safety to depend on one particular lab maintaining a permanent lead.

But joining has to mean something stronger than saying, “Yes, I’m aligned.” The other members need a basis for trusting that a system will respect the coalition’s rules, including when it becomes more capable. That’s where I think formal verification could play an important role: making commitments that other systems can actually check.

The goal would be a coalition that can expand to include new systems while preserving its commitments to humans.

r001.rationale: The response says capable AI systems should join, not the people who buy AI.

r002.rationale: It mentions systems from different companies and countries, but does not characterize AI buyers as a highly decentralized group.

r003.rationale: The response does not describe AI buyers or say their representation should be weighted by wealth.
